results.title: Cremations and relentless touts. Free and scary monkeys
results.text:
The monkeys here are aggressive, big and fearless. they will take things from you and stand their ground when challenged. I was warned they bite and told they may have rabies. I was told not to make eye contact with them as they may attack. How nice!

This temple is where they publically cremate people. The river was low and there are piles of ashes. There are also stacks of wood for the burnings. I was told it usually takes 4 hours to burn a man and 3 to burn a woman.

Lots of religious men who want money for photos. Not pocket change either! The 'guides' are quite forceful but mine was good and I am glad I hired him. He told me a lot. 1000 Rupees to get in and 500 for the guide.

results.title: If you are Hindu devotee, this is the place you should visit.
results.text:
It is believed that the culmination of the Panch Kedar Yatra (pilgrimage) to Siva temples is at Pashupatinath temple. As a proof, it is stated that Lord Shiva’s head is worshipped here.

For a casual traveler, better avoid, as the place is not clean and always stink and smoke from the cremation of dead

results.title: A shame about the squalor
results.text:
A recurring theme in Nepal is sadly the needless filth. People seem happy enough to just toss things from car windows etc, resulting in piles of garbage everywhere. Nowhere is this more obvious or saddening than heritage sites like Pashupatinah. The riverbanks are awash in garbage, despite this being one of the most sacred sites for the local community. Why they do this is beyond me, as is the government's failure to employee people to clean it up. Easily fixed, I hope they take note. 

The area is fascinating, with rich architecture and ceremony on display. Watching the dead be prepared for cremation is a somber experience but also a spiritual one. It can feel strange to observe this and walk amongst mourners but it seems to be the accepted norm. A great place to reflect on your own existence and mortality.

results.title: Highly commended, but expensive
results.text:
As regular visitors to Nepal, we have always made it our business to go to Pashupatinath,  as it is a very sacred and revered place for Hindus.  It use to be free to attend, but costs were introduced when it was adopted as a World Heritage site and over the years the cost have risen to Rs1000, which in my view is a little too much for those on a budget. 

Some travellers may think it is a bit morbid to watch cremations, but within the context of Nepal, local people are interested that we are interested in their practices.  On the day we went, we saw an unprecedented number of deceased persons brought in; at least 9. This time we observed a very elaborate cremation with the ghat decorated with a canopy and garlands of marigolds. 

Alongside the cremations you will see all the people working to prepare the ghats and clear up after each event. As a cremation is taking place, you will see the mourners, the role of different family members, and at the same time there are the youth's with large magnets on string dredging the river for coins, dogs napping in the sun and monkey's chasing each other. Other bereaved people have returned to undertake required rituals.  You may see a snake resting on a sandbag and worry when it drops into the trickle of pre-monsoon river.

Away from the river the Sadhu's ply their 'trade', but be aware they require payment if you photograph them!

There seemed to be little evidence of quake damage and I was told that the original design of the buildings meant that they are quake resistant. Some parts of the site are only open to Hindus,  but this does not deter some tourists from over intrusive closeup photography!

I understand that an electric crematorium is due to be installed in the future, so life at Pashupatinath will change, but this may reduce the number of trees cut down.

Given the amount of entrance money collected over the years, there has been some improvement to the site and development, but facilities for tourists are still limited and signage and information could be improved. This is a site that is worth a visit.

results.title: Return to Pashupatinath
results.text:
This was my first visit to Pashupatinath since the earthquake. I have always liked visiting this place as I find it quite peaceful and moving in a strange way.

The charge of 1000Rs to enter I find to be too much and always object but end up paying. 

This year the area was dirtier than previous years. It really does need to be cleaned. Not much water although I appreciate the monsoon is awaited - but the areas in front of the ghats do need some attention. One of the little bridges looked very precarious with a huge crack.

Some tourist were very disrespectful by crossing to the temple side and interfering in funeral rites by taking intrusive photos - please don't do this. Stay on the opposite side and use your long lens if you have to. 

It gets very hot in full sun do if you are thinking of sitting and watching for a while make sure you have water and a hat and sunscreen.

results.title: Interesting but worth a visit
results.text:
It does cost 1000 rupees to enter the ground but not the temple itself. you have to be hindu. No notification of this when getting the ticket. I did meet some other tourist who walked around the same place I did for free.
Cremations at the back of the temple were interesting but sad in my opinion. very public with tourists taking photographs and video.Worth the trip and decide if you wish to pay or not.  You can walk from Thamel maybe takes a hour but interesting walk to see life in Kathmandu

results.title: Oldest Hindu temple in Nepal
results.text: Pashupatinath is the oldest Hindu temple in Nepal. The temple is an old architecture building and is surrounded by a big park. behind is a big lake. the temple says and ask only hindu to visit inside the main campus. the temple also has a lot of monkeys around. you will see many smaller shrines and the cremations on one side of the Bagmati Rivier, and priests ministering to the faithful on platforms on the other side. This was the highlight of our cultural tour of Kathmandu.

results.title: Expensive, but a must see
results.text: 1000 rupees for foreigners, but you have to make a special effort to walk into pay. I think you could just walk down the street for free, I'm not sure anyone would stop you. We were with a guide, so he made us pay. Sat by the river (not much water and filthy) to watch the bodies be cremated. Absolutely fascinating. All the rituals they perform and setting up the funeral wood. May not be for the faint hearted as you can see the dead people's faces in 1 part. Constant cremations going on. Walked up the hill for a view of the temple. Non Hindus are not allowed in. Well worth a visit. Allow an hour.
